query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A dual-step process—first inducing an ultrafine-grained (UFG) structure through severe plastic deformation followed by a controlled low-temperature oxidation treatment—accelerates the formation of a continuous, chromium-rich passive film that significantly enhances corrosion resistance in stainless steels under harsh conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Stainless steel with conventional (coarse-grained) microstructure and native oxide films.
generation.intervention: Apply severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-pressure torsion at defined strain rates to achieve grain sizes below 500 nm) followed by a post-deformation oxidation treatment at around 400°C for 2 hours in air to promote uniform Cr diffusion to the surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure to corrosive environments such as high-temperature aqueous solutions or chloride-containing media typical of chemical processing and nuclear power applications.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained microstructure coupled with a post-treatment optimized passive film exhibiting enhanced Cr enrichment and continuity.
generation.mechanism: While UFG structures elevate the grain boundary density and potential for increased Cr diffusion, the additional low-temperature oxidation step ensures that the diffusing Cr is captured into a stable, adherent passivation layer, thereby preventing further corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Stainless steels subjected to the dual-step process will display significantly reduced corrosion current densities, a more uniform and Cr-rich oxide film, and improved long-term corrosion stability compared to steels with either conventional processing or UFG structure alone.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained stainless steels with native passivation behavior and steels processed by severe plastic deformation without subsequent controlled oxidation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is applicable to stainless steels with sufficient Cr content (typically >16%) and under conditions where post-treatment oxidation can be reliably controlled; results might vary if service temperatures induce coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: The precise impact of each treatment step on the overall enhancement of corrosion resistance must be quantified, particularly regarding the longevity of the induced passive film under cyclic stresses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of stainless steel samples: one with conventional processing, one processed to achieve UFG microstructure only, and one undergoing the dual-step process (UFG + low-temperature oxidation). Expose all sets to elevated-temperature chloride environments that simulate chemical processing conditions.
measurements: XPS and SKP to analyze passive film composition and uniformity
Potentiodynamic polarization tests for corrosion current density
Grain size measurements using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-step processed samples do not exhibit a significantly thicker, more chromium-rich passive film and lower corrosion rates compared with both the conventionally processed and UFG-only samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The oxide layer formed on the Al-HEA coating had different composition and structure in comparison with the Mo-HEA oxide layer after the aerated test. The oxide layer on Al-HEA coating was found to have more corrosion damage characteristics rather than passive layer behavior, i.e., not with compact structure. The Al-HEA oxide layer was in some cases detached from the bulk material, and the layer was composed of oxides from all the elements in the HEA as seen in Figure 10. In addition, localized corrosion damage enriched in Al-O was also observed on the surface of the Al-HEA coating in locations where the complex oxide film had not formed to a significant extent as seen in Figure 11. Localized oxide corrosion forms were observed in the aerated test but not in the wellhead test. The Al-O-rich localized damage might suggest that the oxidation of Al has faster kinetics than the oxidation of the other elements. This localized corrosion behavior also strengthens the assumption that the complex oxide film is not passive. Cracks were also observed in the Al-HEA coating in the sample Al-HEA-304L after the exposure in the aerated environment as seen in Figure 12.

The present results for CoCrFeMnNi alloys on the stable passivation composition against UFG formation (or less sensitive composition to grain size than Fe–Cr alloys) can be explained by considering some high-entropy effects, which are among the four core effects of HEAs. The high-entropy effect of HEAs decreases the possibility of elemental segregation or local enrichment of specific elements and favors the formation of a uniform distribution of component elements. Therefore, the selective dissolution of specific elements, which leads to local enrichment of the other remaining elements, increases the mixing enthalpy and may destabilize the fcc phase. The corrosion behavior of UFG CoCrFeMnNi alloys processed by HPT with Cr contents ranging from 0 to 20 at.% was investigated in 3.5% NaCl and 0.5 M H2SO4 solutions and compared to homogenized coarse-grained (CG) counterpart materials. Several conclusions were obtained, as follows. The polarization curves in 1 M H2SO4 solution showed the active–passive, passive and transpassive behavior typical of binary Fe–Cr alloys. An increase in Cr content decreased the potential of the active–passive transition, and thus increased the ability to passivate. Cr was the dominant element providing the passivation ability. The polarization curves in 1 M H2SO4 solution showed little difference between the coarse-grained state after homogenization and the nanocrystalline structure after HPT. The impact of nanocrystalline structure on corrosion was negligibly small. Similarly, corrosion resistance to pitting in 3.5% NaCl solution was also little affected by the formation of the nanocrystalline structure, and this is in striking contrast to the high corrosion resistance of nanocrystalline or ultrafine-grained stainless steels processed by SPD reported elsewhere.
